# Reading function from variation

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/10-variants-qtl.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second
reader.
:::

Genome-wide association studies find places in the genome where variation
tracks a trait. They do not say what the variation does. The standard answer
has been that the variant changes how much of some gene is made, and that
answer works less often than its popularity suggests.

Mediated expression score regression was applied to 42 traits, using GTEx
cis-eQTL data from 48 tissues. It put the share of heritability mediated by
assayed gene expression levels at 11 per cent, reported as 11 plus or minus 2
[@yao2020quantifying]. Most of it is mediated by something else.

## The colocalisation gap {#sec-coloc-gap}

A sharper version of the problem comes from asking the question backwards. One
set of genes was nominated as causal for a complex trait on grounds that have
nothing to do with expression, such as coding variants in the gene or in its
Mendelian counterpart. Those genes were then scored for how often a GTEx eQTL
for them colocalises with the GWAS signal.

Out of 220 such genes, colocalisation implicated 18, which is 8.2 per cent.
Those authors note that this is not clearly better than chance
[@connally2022missing].

The explanation is not a shortage of eQTLs. More than nine in ten of the
candidate causal genes had a detectable eQTL in at least one trait-relevant
tissue [@connally2022missing]. The eQTLs are there, and they are not the same
signal.

![Two views of the same gap. The overlap between the eQTL and sQTL fractions
was not reported, so those bars are drawn side by side rather than stacked. On
the right, the collapse happens at the last step rather than the
earlier ones.](../figures/coloc-gap.svg){#fig-coloc width=100%}

The best-powered resource gives the same picture from the other direction.
Across 5,385 GWAS associations in 1,167 independent LD blocks from 87 complex
traits, GTEx v8 colocalised 43 per cent with a cis-eQTL and 23 per cent with a
cis-splicing QTL [@aguet2019gtex]. A majority of loci have no expression
explanation in the largest multi-tissue dataset available.

## Splicing QTLs are a different map {#sec-qtl-position}

Splicing QTLs are not a relabelling of expression QTLs.

They sit in different parts of the gene. The splicing set was preferentially
enriched at splice acceptor and donor sites and at RNA-binding-protein
footprints. The expression set was enriched at transcription start sites and
lay closer to them [@qi2022genetic].

Where a gene has both, the two usually come from different variants. GTEx v8's
own summary states that where a gene carries both an expression QTL and a
splicing QTL, the two effects are usually driven by different causal variants
[@aguet2019gtex]. Finding one says little about the other at the same gene.

Overlap at gene level is therefore misleading. A multivariate transcript-ratio
analysis of GTEx v7 found 52 per cent of its splicing QTLs were also expression
QTLs for the same gene and tissue. The lead splicing variant and the lead
expression variant were the same SNP in only 3 per cent of cases
[@garridomartin2021identification], so the two maps share genes and almost never
variants.

Allelic expression does not bridge the two either. In GTEx v8 the correlation
between allelic imbalance and splicing-QTL genotype was essentially nil, and
the consortium concluded that genetic splicing variation in cis is not strongly
reflected in gene-level allelic expression data [@aguet2019gtex]. Gene-level
allelic expression is a good proxy for expression QTLs and a poor one for
splicing QTLs.

## What splicing QTLs find {#sec-sqtl-finds}

The argument for them was made early. A study in Yoruba
lymphoblastoid cell lines reported 2,893 splicing QTLs, most of which had little
or no effect on gene-level expression. Those authors judged their aggregate
contribution to complex traits roughly equal to that of variants acting on
expression levels [@li2016splicing].

Brain gave the strongest version of it. In 2,865 human brain transcriptomes,
12,794
genes carried a cis-splicing QTL. For 4,377 of the genes that also had an
expression QTL, the two signals were statistically incompatible, with a
posterior probability above 0.8 for two distinct causal variants. Together with
the splicing-only genes, that put roughly 61 per cent of splicing QTLs outside
the expression QTL map [@qi2022genetic].

The consequence for gene discovery is direct. Integrating those brain splicing
QTLs with GWAS for twelve brain-related traits implicated 244 genes through
splicing, about 61 per cent of which the matched expression QTL data could not
have found [@qi2022genetic].

The same pattern shows up locus by locus in other diseases. A
transcriptome-wide association study of rheumatoid arthritis run on
intron-excision phenotypes named 18 candidate genes, 13 of which the same
analysis on gene expression levels did not find [@li2017annotation].

## How much it explains, stated carefully {#sec-how-much}

The case above is easy to overstate, and the same datasets support a more
measured reading.

GWAS catalog variants in GTEx v8 were enriched 1.46-fold among cis-eQTLs and
1.86-fold among cis-splicing QTLs. The splicing QTLs are the smaller annotation,
20 per cent of tested variants against 43 per cent [@aguet2019gtex], so the
per-variant enrichment favours splicing.

The consortium's own reading of that is cautious. Under the robust enrichment
analyses
the relative GWAS enrichments of splicing and expression QTLs were similar and
not significantly different, and because far more expression QTLs were
discovered, the consortium inferred a greater aggregated contribution from them
[@aguet2019gtex].

Partitioning heritability by annotation gives the same shape. In blood, the
roughly 1.0 per cent of SNPs annotated as expression QTLs explained 13.9 per
cent of heritability on average across traits. The much smaller splicing-QTL
annotation, 0.1 per cent of SNPs, explained 2.8 per cent, and protein QTLs, 0.2
per cent of SNPs, explained 4.0 per cent [@liu2025transcriptional].

The literature does not agree on how to weigh this. The authors of the
colocalisation audit dismissed splicing QTLs as a candidate explanation for
their negative result, on the grounds that splicing QTLs consistently explain
less phenotypic variance than expression QTLs [@connally2022missing]. That is
the opposite emphasis from the lymphoblastoid and brain work above. The
disagreement is about aggregate variance explained, and it is unresolved.

Per variant, splicing QTLs are at least as informative, and in total there are
fewer of them, with both statements coming from the same data.

## Isoform-level QTLs {#sec-isoform-qtl}

Splicing QTLs are still measured on events rather than on molecules. Moving to
isoform-level phenotypes changes what is detectable again, and
@sec-gtex-lr gives the long-read result that makes the point most sharply.

Two configurations are worth naming, because they are the ones a gene-level
analysis cannot represent. Within that B-cell isoform QTL set, 1,135 variants
had significantly different effect sizes on different isoforms of the same
gene, and 153 pushed two isoforms in opposite directions
[@nagura2025longread]. Summing isoform counts into a gene total cancels the
second configuration exactly.

The mechanisms are not only splice-signal disruption. Variants found only by
isoform-level mapping in B cells were enriched at intronic branchpoints, and
also at promoters and super-enhancers [@nagura2025longread]. An isoform QTL can
be a transcription-initiation choice.

Short reads can reach some of this if the phenotype is defined well. Mapping
isoform-to-gene expression ratios rather than isoform abundances, in 2,622
Framingham whole-blood samples, yielded over 1.1 million common cis
associations. A fifth of those had no significant association with overall gene
expression. The same analysis found 1,870 sentinel trans associations
[@liu2025integrating]. Isoform-ratio QTLs act at a distance as well as locally.

Poly(A) site choice is a mappable phenotype in its own right. Three-prime-end
sequencing of nuclear RNA from lymphoblastoid lines identified 602
polyadenylation QTLs in 479 genes, with lead variants clustered near the
poly(A) sites whose usage they changed [@mittleman2020alternative].

Association testing shows the same kind of gain. Running transcriptome-wide
association
tests on isoform rather than gene expression, across six cancers and six
subtype classifications, raised the number of significant associations from
2,336 to 6,163. It tagged associations at 52 per cent more independent GWAS
loci, and attributed an estimated 63 per cent greater share of cancer risk SNP
heritability to isoform expression than to gene expression
[@chang2025isoform]. Specific loci make it concrete: CLPTM1L in lung, LAMC1 in
colorectal and BABAM1 in breast cancer colocalise with an isoform-level
association and not with a gene-level one [@chang2025isoform].

One caution belongs here, from the B-cell study itself. Of 372 variants
coinciding with a published GWAS association, 242 were found only by the
isoform-level analysis. The per-variant GWAS hit rate was 2.0 per cent for
isoform-only variants, against 2.4 per cent for shared ones and 0.8 per cent
for gene-only ones [@nagura2025longread]. The 242 reflects a much larger
isoform-only pool rather than a higher enrichment per variant.

More associations is not automatically more signal. The case for isoform-level
mapping rests on the configurations gene-level analysis cannot represent.

## From uncertain significance to an answer {#sec-vus}

Clinical variant interpretation has the same problem in a form where a single
patient's result depends on it.

The ACMG/AMP framework already asks whether a variant perturbs splicing, and
spreads that question across six evidence codes: PVS1, PS3, PP3, BS3, BP4 and
BP7. As of the ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation splicing subgroup's
review there was no standardised method for turning RNA data into any of them,
which is why expert panels had diverged [@walker2023application].

What RNA evidence does to a backlog has been modelled. Treating RNA evidence as
one supporting-strength point in a semiquantitative implementation, a clinical
laboratory projected that 31 per cent of its 16,965 unique splicing variants of
uncertain significance would cross a classification threshold. Of those, 93 per
cent would land on the benign side and 7 per cent on the pathogenic side
[@truty2021spectrum]. That describes where variants sit relative to
thresholds, rather than observed RNA results.

RNA evidence rarely settles a case on its own. For 69 per cent of that cohort's
unique splicing variants of uncertain significance, a classification would
still fall short, because no other applicable evidence category existed to
combine with the RNA result [@truty2021spectrum].

Three constraints bound what the assay can see. The transcripts are read in part
rather than whole. RT-PCR and both targeted and whole-transcriptome RNA-seq
report which splicing events occurred, and not the complete exon structure of
the resulting mRNA, and comprehensive long-read data is still lacking for many
disease-susceptibility genes [@walker2023application]. The tissue has to contain
the transcript, and pathogenic splicing variants detected in fibroblasts have
been reported as undetected in blood [@peymani2022rna]. The variant class that
most needs observing is also the one decay removes. Nonsense, frameshift and
often canonical splice-site variants introduce premature termination codons and
trigger nonsense-mediated decay, which is likely to leave the affected
transcript at a very low expression level [@peymani2022rna].

Allele-specific expression modifies the picture for coding variants. Allelic
imbalance has been put at 30 per cent or more of genes in a given cell type.
Measured with targeted deep sequencing in ten tissues of one individual, allelic
ratios varied across tissues more than gene expression levels did
[@kukurba2014allelic].

## Transcriptomes in the clinic {#sec-clinical}

Expression-based assays are already in clinical use. The PAM50 breast cancer
signature
was retrained on a 50-gene counting platform for formalin-fixed material,
cleared by the FDA and CE marked, and issued for decentralised use in clinical
laboratories as a recurrence-risk and intrinsic-subtype test
[@wallden2015development].

Fusion detection is where RNA changes the diagnosis rather than annotating it.
In a 788-patient multicentre sarcoma cohort, adding targeted RNA fusion
sequencing to histopathology changed the pathological subtype for 11.9 per cent
of patients, and confirmed or refined the diagnosis for a further 13.3 per cent
[@jin2025superiority].

Against DNA-based panels over shared fusion targets, the RNA panel reached 93.5
per cent sensitivity and
98.8 per cent specificity, and orthogonal testing of DNA-only fusion calls
indicated several were non-functional events [@jin2025superiority]. Sample
quality is the binding constraint, and it is reported as a number: roughly 40
per cent of heavily degraded specimens were still successfully profiled
[@jin2025superiority].

The honest summary of adoption comes from a 2025 validation of an integrated
tumour DNA-plus-RNA exome assay. It describes RNA-seq as the standard way to
measure fusions and characterise tissue phenotype, while stating in the same
sentence that its clinical adoption remains limited [@yudina2025clinical].

A variant whose effect is invisible in gene-level expression and unambiguous in
isoform usage is a variant that gene-level analysis calls silent. The methods
for seeing it exist, and what they still lack is a standardised path from an RNA
observation to a classification code.
